title: RENAME
description: Rename persistent object labels deliberately, distinguish query aliases from DDL, and verify preserved data without assuming consumers or concurrent workloads are automatically compatible.
notes:
## A persistent rename changes the object interface

Renaming a table changes the name through which callers identify it. A campus project might rename pupil_records to student_records to match the institution's current terminology. The existing rows are not meant to become different students, and the identifier values should not be regenerated. The requested change is a persistent object label, rather than a new population or a query-only nickname.

A SQL alias has a narrower scope. SELECT statements can refer to student_records as s without changing the stored table name. ALTER TABLE or a product-specific rename statement changes the persistent definition. Keeping those scopes separate prevents a common mistake: assuming AS in one query migrates every later caller to a new table name.

## Inspect the final name and preserved state

The basic postcondition is that the intended object is accessible under the new name with its relevant definition and rows preserved. A report after the rename can verify the retained identifiers and values. It should not insert replacement students merely to make the result resemble the old sample. That would be a data-copy redesign rather than the requested renaming operation.

Constraints and indexes also matter, but preserved rows alone do not prove every dependent property stayed correct. A meaningful review identifies which properties the actual engine preserves and which references need changes. A table can still contain all its old rows while an external report fails because it continues to use the previous spelling.

```sql
ALTER TABLE old_labels RENAME TO current_labels;
```

## Dialects expose different rename forms

MySQL supports RENAME TABLE for applicable table renames and ALTER TABLE forms for relevant object changes. PostgreSQL has its own ALTER TABLE RENAME forms. SQL Server uses sp_rename for appropriate operations. A script must use the supported syntax and object rules of its target rather than substitute names into a single supposedly universal statement.

Temporary objects can have additional restrictions. In the MySQL-style exercises, ALTER TABLE is used to rename the supplied temporary tables. That is deliberate: a successful temporary-table ALTER does not prove every RENAME TABLE form accepts temporary objects. State the actual operation exercised instead of labeling all statements with the same broad word and assuming their support is identical.

## Column renames affect a different interface role

Renaming a column changes the name consumers use to refer to a property. A table can preserve the same values while an application mapper expecting old_email fails to read contact_email. Consumers include handwritten SQL, report definitions, imports, serialization code and generated model assumptions. Search actual callers before concluding that a metadata-only change is application-transparent.

A query can expose an output alias for gradual presentation changes, but an alias in one view or report does not update every stored or external reference. A compatibility strategy needs a defined consumer population and expected behaviour. Do not assume that a renamed database object automatically rewrites application source files or every dynamic SQL string.

## Dependency updates are product specific

Some catalog-tracked relationships can follow internal object identities through supported renames. Other references depend on stored SQL text or external names. Views, routines, grants, triggers and foreign keys have their own product-specific behaviour. The phrase dependencies are preserved is too broad unless it names the kinds of dependencies and the exact supported operation being discussed.

An old view is not a reliable compatibility bridge merely because it existed before the rename. Its definition and behaviour need inspection on the target product. Likewise, manually recreating a bridge does not establish correct privileges or updateability automatically. The important lesson is to verify the dependent contract rather than infer all reference handling from the preservation of base-table rows.

## A compatibility view needs a concrete consumer contract

A team can sometimes expose an old name as a view selecting from the newly named table. That can help selected readers transition when the columns, access rules and query semantics remain compatible. An explicit selected column list states the intended interface more clearly than relying on an uncontrolled star expansion over a changing definition.

Such a view is not automatically a complete substitute for the original table. Write operations, generated-key retrieval, metadata inspection and application tooling can have different requirements. Privilege and view-security behaviour also need deliberate choices. Explain which old uses are supported and test those uses instead of promising that a single view makes every historical client work unchanged.

## A cheap metadata change can still wait

A rename may avoid copying the table's full row population in supported cases. That does not guarantee instant completion under load. Metadata locks or other coordination can cause waiting, and an operation can affect concurrent statements even when the table's data bytes do not require a rewrite. Physical work and user-visible interruption are different dimensions.

Cross-database moves or other combined operations can introduce additional restrictions and cost. Do not generalize from a same-database rename to every possible object relocation. A three-row lab can validate the final visible name and content; it cannot establish production lock duration or an operational no-downtime guarantee. Those claims need their own workload and engine evidence.

## Name collisions need an explicit transition

If current_labels already exists, renaming old_labels to that occupied name cannot simply be treated as an overwrite of an unrelated table. Decide what each object represents and which final names are intended. A temporary transition name can distinguish the roles during a controlled single-session swap, but every step has its own observable state.

The second exercise demonstrates such a staged swap on disposable temporary tables. It does not claim the three statements are one atomic operation for concurrent consumers. MySQL's supported multi-table RENAME TABLE behaviour is a different native operation with its own object restrictions. Students should see that a pedagogical sequential trace and an atomic production name switch are not interchangeable guarantees.

## A rename does not archive or validate data

Changing the table name to archived_records does not move rows to an archival policy automatically. It does not apply retention rules, change access grants correctly for every actor, or prove that the data should no longer be edited. A label can communicate intent, but enforcement requires the actual definitions and trusted application rules that implement that intent.

Likewise, renaming amount to total does not make an incorrect calculation correct or change a currency unit. Property semantics follow the recorded facts and operations, not the prettiness of a label. A good migration explanation connects the new name with the same underlying meaning or explicitly describes any semantic change as a separate requirement.

## Preserve identifiers while testing the new reference

The introductory task renames one temporary table and reads its unchanged item identifiers and labels. Hidden cases include a different identity, repeated labels and no rows. Those cases prevent a reference solution from recreating only the original sample data under the new name. The operation must preserve the supplied state rather than memorize the example.

The swap task starts with blue and green table roles containing different markers. A temporary transition name makes the sequence traceable. Afterward, reading each final name should yield the other original role's rows. Repeated values remain repeated occurrences because a rename does not imply DISTINCT. Empty input on one side should move as an empty population without inventing a marker.

## Do not equate reversibility with compatibility

A rename can sometimes be reversed by another supported rename if the required names remain available. That does not undo effects in consumers that failed, cached stale assumptions or wrote to a changed interface during the transition. A rollback description needs the full application state it intends to recover, rather than only a reverse spelling of the DDL command.

For these exercises, the objects are single-session and disposable, so the observable contract is deliberately narrow. They teach name transition, state preservation and collision handling without claiming production recovery evidence. The prepared content migrations only store the explanatory packages and assessment definitions; they do not execute these instructional table operations against application data.

## Report what the rename fixtures actually establish

A useful structural illustration lists the old name, intermediate name where applicable, final name and preserved source identity. That makes it easier to detect accidental overwrites or copies. Review the operation form and object kind alongside that trace. The right final labels are not enough when the row populations have been swapped incorrectly or an unrelated object has been touched.

Recorded MariaDB fixtures verify the supplied temporary-table ALTER sequences and final outputs. Exact MySQL/provider execution, native multi-object rename atomicity, dependent-object behaviour and production locking remain separate checks. Preserving these distinctions lets a complete learning package teach practical naming changes without making unsupported promises about every caller, engine or concurrent workload.

questions.question_text: What is preserved when you rename a table using ALTER TABLE ... RENAME TO?
options: The data and indexes; only the object's name changes
Only the indexes, not the data
Only the data, not the indexes
questions.explanation: Renaming updates the catalog's name mapping while data and indexes remain intact.

questions.question_text: Which SQL Server procedure is used to rename a table or column?
questions.explanation: SQL Server uses the sp_rename system stored procedure for renaming objects.

questions.question_text: Why review dependent view and routine definitions after a table rename?
options: The view is automatically renamed too
Name-based or stored references may not remain compatible automatically under the target engine
MySQL blocks all renames if any view exists
Views are unaffected in every MySQL version
questions.explanation: Avoid an unsupported claim tied only to older MySQL SELECT-star caching.

questions.question_text: When might an old-name compatibility view help?
options: When its tested interface supports the intended old readers during a defined migration
Because views are required by SQL syntax after a rename
questions.explanation: It does not automatically preserve every write, metadata or access behaviour.

questions.question_text: Does avoiding a row-copy rewrite guarantee an instant rename?
options: No; metadata locking and operation-specific restrictions can still matter
Only if the table has more than one index
questions.explanation: Physical row-copy cost and observed interruption differ.

questions.question_text: What is a real risk when renaming a column that is used inside stored procedures or ORM model definitions?
options: No risk — all references update automatically everywhere
Those references are not automatically updated and can cause runtime errors discovered later
The stored procedures are automatically deleted
The rename operation itself will fail immediately
questions.explanation: A rename doesn't retroactively fix hardcoded references in procedures, triggers, or application code.

questions.question_text: Why can a metadata-based rename still affect busy workloads?
options: It requires a full table scan
Coordination and metadata-lock waits can block or delay supported operations
It always drops and recreates all indexes
questions.explanation: Do not promise a universally brief exclusive lock interval.

questions.question_text: In general, do foreign key constraints continue to function correctly after the referenced table is renamed?
options: No, foreign keys are always dropped by a rename
Generally yes, since most engines track the relationship by internal object identity rather than by name alone, but this should be verified per engine/version
Only if the constraint is manually recreated after every rename
questions.explanation: Most engines track foreign keys internally rather than purely by name, so they typically survive a rename, though verification per engine is wise.

questions.question_text: Does a SELECT alias persistently rename a table?
questions.explanation: Aliases label query roles.

questions.question_text: What must a state-preserving rename retain?
options: The intended rows and identifiers under the new reference
questions.explanation: Name transition is not arbitrary data replacement.

questions.question_text: What does an occupied destination name require?
questions.explanation: Both objects may have meaningful independent identity.

questions.question_text: Does a sequential three-step swap prove concurrent atomicity?
questions.explanation: Intermediate states exist in the demonstrated sequence.

questions.question_text: Why use ALTER TABLE for temporary-table rename practice?
options: The supported object rules differ from some RENAME TABLE forms
All forms accept all object kinds
questions.explanation: The exercised syntax must match the object kind.

questions.question_text: Does renaming a table to archive enforce a retention policy?
questions.explanation: Labels do not implement access and retention rules.

questions.question_text: Why test a renamed column’s callers?
options: Applications may still reference the prior property name
questions.explanation: External consumers lie outside automatic catalog handling.

questions.question_text: What does an explicit compatibility-view column list clarify?
questions.explanation: The view still needs supported behaviour and permissions.

questions.question_text: Do repeated rows disappear because a table was renamed?
questions.explanation: Rename does not change occurrence multiplicity.

questions.question_text: Can a reverse rename alone prove full application rollback?
questions.explanation: Failures and writes during transition have their own state effects.

questions.question_text: Which evidence supports a no-interruption production claim?
questions.explanation: Metadata changes can still coordinate with active users.

questions.question_text: What does the staged swap preserve explicitly?
options: Each original source population under its intended final name
questions.explanation: The trace follows source identity through each step.

coding_problems.title: Rename the supplied temporary table without replacing its rows
coding_problems.task: Use ALTER TABLE to rename TEMPORARY old_labels to current_labels. Return item_id and label from current_labels without changing supplied rows.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE old_labels (item_id INT PRIMARY KEY, label VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL);
constraints: Use the supplied temporary object only.
edge_cases: An empty table remains empty under the new name.
Repeated labels with different identifiers remain distinct rows.
hints: ALTER the existing object rather than copying a memorized sample.
coding_problems.solution_sql: ALTER TABLE old_labels RENAME TO current_labels; SELECT item_id,label FROM current_labels ORDER BY item_id;
coding_problems.explanation: The same supplied population becomes accessible through its new table name.

coding_problems.title: Trace a single-session temporary name swap
coding_problems.task: In this disposable single-session exercise, swap the names of TEMPORARY blue and green using a free transition name swap_hold and ALTER TABLE statements. Return final_name and marker from both final names, preserving all occurrences. This staged sequence is not asserted atomic for concurrent consumers.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE blue (marker VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL); CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE green (marker VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL);
coding_problems.seed_sql: INSERT INTO blue VALUES ('B1'),('B2'); INSERT INTO green VALUES ('G1');
coding_problems.expected:
final_name	marker
blue	G1
green	B1
green	B2
constraints: The transition name is initially unoccupied.
Do not modify source marker values.
hints: Free the occupied destination by moving the first table to the transition name.
Track source populations after each step.
coding_problems.solution_sql: ALTER TABLE blue RENAME TO swap_hold; ALTER TABLE green RENAME TO blue; ALTER TABLE swap_hold RENAME TO green; SELECT 'blue' AS final_name,marker FROM blue UNION ALL SELECT 'green' AS final_name,marker FROM green ORDER BY final_name,marker;
coding_problems.explanation: The transition name resolves the collision while the selected final labels expose where each source population ended.

validation_cases.expected:
final_name	marker
green	B
green	B

original_questions.question_text: Which SQL Server procedure is used to rename a table or column?

original_questions.question_text: What is a documented risk of renaming a table in older MySQL versions when views reference it with SELECT *?
options: The view is automatically renamed too
The view may break or behave unexpectedly because its definition was resolved/cached at creation time
MySQL blocks all renames if any view exists
Views are unaffected in every MySQL version
original_questions.explanation: Dependent views can be a pitfall of renaming, especially historically in MySQL, since their column resolution was cached.

original_questions.question_text: Why might a team create a compatibility view (e.g., CREATE VIEW employees AS SELECT * FROM staff) after renaming a table?
options: To let old code using the old table name keep working during a gradual migration
Because views are required by SQL syntax after a rename
original_questions.explanation: A compatibility view provides a soft transition period instead of forcing an immediate, all-at-once cutover of every caller.

original_questions.question_text: Does renaming a table typically require rewriting the table's physical data files?
options: No — it is usually a metadata-only catalog change, so it is fast
Only if the table has more than one index
original_questions.explanation: Renaming just updates the name-to-object mapping in most engines, which is why it's typically near-instant.

original_questions.question_text: What is a real risk when renaming a column that is used inside stored procedures or ORM model definitions?
options: No risk — all references update automatically everywhere
Those references are not automatically updated and can cause runtime errors discovered later
The stored procedures are automatically deleted
The rename operation itself will fail immediately
original_questions.explanation: A rename doesn't retroactively fix hardcoded references in procedures, triggers, or application code.

original_questions.question_text: Even though a rename is usually metadata-only, why might it still momentarily affect concurrent queries on a busy table?
options: It requires a full table scan
Most engines still take a brief exclusive lock during the rename
It always drops and recreates all indexes
original_questions.explanation: A short exclusive lock is typically required even for a metadata-only rename, which can briefly block concurrent access.

original_questions.question_text: In general, do foreign key constraints continue to function correctly after the referenced table is renamed?
options: No, foreign keys are always dropped by a rename
Generally yes, since most engines track the relationship by internal object identity rather than by name alone, but this should be verified per engine/version
Only if the constraint is manually recreated after every rename
original_questions.explanation: Most engines track foreign keys internally rather than purely by name, so they typically survive a rename, though verification per engine is wise.
